title: Writing HCL for our modules

story: DevOps asks you for a change in the sandbox pool module: routines such as the CI fixer can retry when a machine disappears, so they should also get groups of Spot machines, which are much cheaper but which AWS can reclaim with a two-minute warning. You open modules/aws-sandbox-pool and find a hundred and fifty lines of HCL full of for_each, each.key, merge and square brackets.

Three groups of VMs already run from this module, and Nova's runs claim machines from them every day. A small mistake here does not throw a red error. It quietly gives the full group the lite machine, or replaces the group, together with its warm VMs, at the next apply.
hook.question: How do I read a module I did not write, and change it without breaking the things that already run from it?

p: A module is easiest to read from its edges. Its variables are its inputs, like a React component's props, and its outputs are what it gives back, like a function's return value. Everything in between is how it does the job. So start with variables.tf and outputs.tf. They tell you what the callers can set, which values are allowed, and what other units read from the module through a dependency.

Each variable has a type, and some have a validation: a condition that must be true, and the error message to show when it is not. The check runs before any plan, so a wrong value stops at your desk, not in AWS. In our pool module, a warm pool can hold 0 to 3 stopped VMs, because each group's max_size is 3. A warm pool of 5 would never fill up, and nobody would notice until runs started waiting for machines.

When you change a module, the contract is the part to protect. Adding an optional variable is safe. Renaming a variable or an output breaks every unit that sets or reads it, and you will only see the break when someone plans that unit.

notes.text: The map's keys become the sizes: one launch template and one group per key.
alltrue([for n in values(...) : ...]) checks every number in the map.
Your message, shown when a caller passes a bad value. Write it for the person who will read it.
An output, keyed by size, so another unit can read asg_names["lite"].

p: Inside the module, almost everything is keyed by size. The launch template block has for_each = var.sizes, so OpenTofu makes one template per key, with addresses like aws_launch_template.sandbox["lite"]. The group block uses the same for_each, and it finds its own template with aws_launch_template.sandbox[each.key]. That one expression is what ties lite's group to lite's template. var.warm_pool_size[each.key] reads the warm pool size for the same key, and if the map has no entry for a size, the plan fails, which is what you want.

Because the key is part of the address, a key is an identity, not a label. Rename full to standard in the sizes map and OpenTofu does not see a rename. It sees that full is gone and standard is new, so it plans to destroy the full template and the full group, warm VMs included, and create new ones. Read a for_each key the way you read a database primary key.

code.file: modules/aws-sandbox-pool: the template and the group (trimmed)

notes.text: One template per key of the map.
each.key goes into the name, so the AWS name also depends on the key.
The image ID is read from a parameter when a VM starts, so promoting a new image changes no HCL (lesson p4-4).
The same key picks the matching template: lite's group launches lite's template.
A map lookup by key. A size with no warm pool entry fails the plan.

read.see:
$ tofu plan   (after renaming the key full to standard, in the lab copy)
  # module.pool.local_file.launch_template["full"] will be destroyed
  # (because key ["full"] is not in for_each map)
  # module.pool.local_file.launch_template["standard"] will be created
  # module.pool.terraform_data.group["full"] will be destroyed
  # module.pool.terraform_data.group["standard"] will be created
Plan: 3 to add, 0 to change, 3 to destroy.

p: The rest of a module is mostly small expressions that reshape maps and lists. Three of them appear in almost every module we have. merge() combines maps, and when two maps have the same key, the later one wins, so the account's tags come first and the module's own tags are added on top. A for expression builds a new map or list from another one, much like .map() in TypeScript. With an if at the end it also filters, like .filter(), which is exactly what the Spot groups need: every size except wide.

You do not have to guess what an expression returns. tofu console is a small interactive shell, like the Node REPL, where you type an expression and see its value. Try an expression there before you put it into a module.

notes.text: The sweeper finds VMs by ai-agents:managed, and the claim code by ai-agents:size.
for <key>, <value> in <map> : <new key> => <new value>. The braces make a map; square brackets would make a list.
The if keeps an entry only when the condition is true.

p: Some settings in a resource are nested blocks, not arguments, and a block cannot take a list. A Spot group, for example, lists its allowed machine types as repeated override { instance_type = ... } blocks. A dynamic block writes one nested block per item: dynamic "override" { for_each = ["m8i", "m7i", "m6i"]  content { instance_type = replace(each.value, "m8i", override.value) } }. Inside content, the current item is named after the block, here override.value.
Use dynamic blocks only when the number of blocks really varies. A fixed set of blocks is easier to read written out.

read.h: Prove the change before the PR
p: A plan shows what a change does with today's inputs. It does not show that the module still keeps its promises with other inputs, such as a new size or a bad warm pool value. For that, OpenTofu has tofu test. You write .tftest.hcl files next to the module, each with one or more run blocks. A run block plans or applies the module with the variables you give it and then checks assert conditions, or expects a validation to fail. command = plan means nothing is created, so the tests are fast and safe.

The test below holds the two promises from this lesson: each group uses its own template, and a warm pool of 5 is refused. If someone later writes ["lite"] where each.key belongs, the plan still looks normal, but the test fails with your message.

notes.text: Variables for every run in the file, like default props for a test.
Plan only. Nothing is written to disk or to AWS.
Compare the group's template with the template of the same size.
Override one variable for this run only.
This run passes only if the validation on warm_pool_size fails.

read.see:
$ tofu test
tests/pool.tftest.hcl... pass
  run "each_group_uses_its_own_template"... pass
  run "warm_pool_over_three_is_refused"... pass

Success! 2 passed, 0 failed.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the other two modules
p: modules/aws-vpc-private builds the sandbox network. It wraps a public registry module, terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws, pinned at version 6.5.1, and sets the inputs that make it private: three /18 subnets cut from the VPC range with cidrsubnet, no public subnets, no internet gateway and no NAT gateway. Its own resources add an S3 endpoint whose policy, written with jsonencode(), allows only our buckets.

modules/aws-egress-proxy is the one place in the account with a road to the internet: two small /28 subnets cut from the spare fourth /18, an internet gateway, and a route table that sends 0.0.0.0/0 there. squid.conf is rendered from a template with templatefile(). Lesson p4-5 explains why the proxy exists and what it allows.

lab.title: Change a copy of the sandbox pool and prove it
needs: OpenTofu 1.10 or newer (tofu test and tofu console are built in). With Terraform 1.6 or newer, the same commands work with terraform.
No cloud account: the lab module writes files and stores values instead of creating AWS resources, but it has the same variables, keys and validation as the real one.
lab.goal: Read a copy of the sandbox pool module from its contract, add Spot groups for lite and full, and prove with tofu test that each group still uses its own template.

guess.q: The pool module has for_each = var.sizes on both the templates and the groups. You rename the key full to standard in the sizes map and in warm_pool_size, and change nothing else. What does the plan show for the full group?

options.text: ~ update in place: the group gets a new name.
options.why: The key is part of the address. To OpenTofu, group["full"] and group["standard"] are two different resources.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the instance type is still m8i.2xlarge.
options.why: The value stayed the same, but the identity changed. OpenTofu tracks resources by address, not by value.

options.text: The full group is destroyed and a standard group is created.
options.why: The old key is no longer in the map, so its resources are destroyed, and the new key gets new ones. In AWS that would destroy the group with its warm VMs.

follow.say: Make the lab folder and paste this block, because it writes a small copy of the pool module (variables.tf, main.tf, outputs.tf) and a root main.tf that calls it with our three sizes.
Read the module from its edges first, the way the Understand step suggests, and then download the provider. init also finds the module folder.
follow.do:
cat modules/sandbox-pool/variables.tf modules/sandbox-pool/outputs.tf
tofu init | grep -E 'pool|Installed|initialized'
follow.see:
- pool in modules/sandbox-pool
- Installed hashicorp/local v2.5.3 (signed, key ID 0C0AF313E5FD9F80)
OpenTofu has been successfully initialized!

follow.say: Plan, apply, and look at the addresses, because every resource inside a module starts with module.<name>.
follow.do:
tofu plan | grep -E '^  #|Plan:'
tofu apply -auto-approve | tail -5
follow.see:
# module.pool.local_file.launch_template["full"] will be created
  …
  # module.pool.terraform_data.group["wide"] will be created
Plan: 6 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
group_names = {
  "full" = "ai-agents-sandbox-full"
  "lite" = "ai-agents-sandbox-lite"
  "wide" = "ai-agents-sandbox-wide"
}

follow.say: Break the contract on purpose: in main.tf set wide = 5 in warm_pool_size and plan, because the validation should stop it before anything happens. Then set it back to 0.
follow.see:
Error: Invalid value for variable

  on main.tf line 6, in module "pool":
   6:   warm_pool_size = { lite = 2, full = 2, wide = 5 }

A warm pool holds 0 to 3 VMs (the group's max_size is 3).

This was checked by the validation rule at
modules/sandbox-pool/variables.tf:12,3-13.

follow.say: Try the filter you will need for the Spot groups in tofu console before you write it into the module, because a wrong expression is easier to see here than in a plan.
follow.do:
echo '{ for k, v in { lite = "m8i.xlarge", full = "m8i.2xlarge", wide = "m8i.4xlarge" } : k => v if k != "wide" }' | tofu console
echo '[for t in ["m8i", "m7i", "m6i"] : replace("m8i.2xlarge", "m8i", t)]' | tofu console

follow.say: Save the test file from the Understand step as modules/sandbox-pool/tests/pool.tftest.hcl and run it inside the module folder, because tofu test tests the module it runs in.
follow.do: cd modules/sandbox-pool && tofu init > /dev/null && tofu test
follow.see:
tests/pool.tftest.hcl... pass
  run "each_group_uses_its_own_template"... pass
  run "warm_pool_over_three_is_refused"... pass

Success! 2 passed, 0 failed.

lab.build: Add Spot groups to the module in a new file, modules/sandbox-pool/spot.tf. Write a terraform_data "spot_group" with one entry per size except wide. Its input holds a name ending in -spot (ai-agents-sandbox-lite-spot), the launch template of the same size, a list of three allowed machine types (m8i, m7i and m6i of the same size, built with replace) and on_demand_pct = 0. Add an output spot_group_names keyed by size. Then add a third run block to the test file that passes all three sizes and asserts that the Spot groups are exactly full and lite. Finish with tofu test in the module folder and tofu plan in ~/academy-labs/p4-3.
checks: tofu test in modules/sandbox-pool says Success! 3 passed, 0 failed.
tofu plan in ~/academy-labs/p4-3 says Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy, and both new addresses are module.pool.terraform_data.spot_group[...] for full and lite.
The plan shows instance_types for full as m8i.2xlarge, m7i.2xlarge and m6i.2xlarge.
There is no spot_group["wide"] anywhere in the plan.
You did not change variables.tf: the module's contract for existing callers is the same.

solution.file: modules/sandbox-pool/spot.tf, plus this run block at the end of tests/pool.tftest.hcl

lab.fix: A teammate "simplifies" modules/sandbox-pool/main.tf: in the group, local_file.launch_template[each.key].filename becomes local_file.launch_template["lite"].filename. Make the same change and run tofu plan in ~/academy-labs/p4-3: it shows only 2 to change, in place, which looks harmless. In AWS it would mean the full and wide groups start lite machines, and Nova's big tickets run out of memory. Run tofu test in the module folder: it fails with "The full group must launch the full template." Put each.key back and run the test again.
explain: Why do you start reading a module at variables.tf and outputs.tf, and what makes a change to them risky?
Why is renaming a for_each key not a rename to OpenTofu, and what does the plan do instead?
The broken ["lite"] reference produced a plan of 2 in-place changes. Why did tofu test catch what the plan did not make obvious?
lab.done: tofu test passes three runs, the plan adds exactly two Spot groups, and you ran tofu destroy -auto-approve in ~/academy-labs/p4-3 at the end.

check.q: A caller passes warm_pool_size = { lite = 2, full = 2, wide = 5 } to the pool module. When does the mistake show?

options.text: At apply, when AWS refuses a warm pool larger than the group.
options.why: The module's validation runs before any plan, so it never reaches AWS.

options.text: At plan time, before anything is created, with the module's own error message.
options.why: A validation block is part of the module's contract. A bad value stops the plan with the message the module author wrote.

options.text: Never: the warm pool simply stays below 5.
options.why: Without the validation that would be the risk. With it, the plan fails right away.

check.q: Why does aws_launch_template.sandbox[each.key] matter inside the group block?

options.text: It makes each group launch the template of its own size, so lite's group starts lite machines.
options.why: Both blocks use the same keys. Looking up the template by each.key is what connects the group and the template of the same size.

options.text: It is needed only for formatting; aws_launch_template.sandbox would also work.
options.why: With for_each, aws_launch_template.sandbox is a map of three templates. A group needs exactly one.

options.text: It creates a new template for each group.
options.why: It only refers to a template that the launch template block already creates. References never create anything.

check.q: A teammate renames the sizes key full to standard "to make it clearer" and says the plan should be a no-op. What will the plan really do?

options.text: Update the full group's name in place.
options.why: OpenTofu tracks resources by address, and the address contains the key. There is nothing to update; the old address simply disappears.

options.text: Nothing, because the instance types are the same.
options.why: The values are the same, but the identities are not. A key is like a primary key.

options.text: Destroy the full template and group, warm VMs included, and create new ones called standard.
options.why: Keys are identities. Renaming one means destroy and create, which is why you treat for_each keys like database primary keys.

p: Three modules in RhinoHealth/infrastructure hold the sandbox infrastructure. modules/aws-vpc-private wraps terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws 6.5.1 with no internet gateway, no NAT and three /18 subnets, and adds an S3 endpoint that only reaches our buckets. modules/aws-sandbox-pool holds one launch template and one Auto Scaling group per size (lite m8i.xlarge, full m8i.2xlarge, wide m8i.4xlarge), the warm pools (lite 2, full 2, wide 0 to start), and Spot groups for lite and full with m8i, m7i and m6i overrides. modules/aws-egress-proxy holds the Squid proxy, the only route out in the VPC.

Tags matter beyond tidiness: the sweeper finds machines by ai-agents:managed and the claim code by ai-agents:size, so a merge() that drops them would leave VMs nobody cleans up. Before a module PR, run what CI runs (tofu fmt -check and terragrunt hcl format --check), then validate and plan the units that use the module.

tickets.why: The launch templates: for_each over sizes, metadata rules, encrypted disk, tags through merge() in a dynamic block.
The groups: the same keys, warm pools from a map, the finish-setup hook, and the Spot groups you built in the lab.
aws-vpc-private: a registry module at a pinned version, private subnets from cidrsubnet, an S3 endpoint policy with jsonencode().
aws-egress-proxy: two /28 subnets, the only internet route, and squid.conf from templatefile().

words.plain: A condition inside a variable block that must be true, with the error message shown before any plan when it is not.
A value a module gives back, like a return value; other units read it through a dependency.
{ for k, v in map : k => v } builds a new map or list from another; an if at the end filters entries.
Combines maps into one; for the same key, the later map wins.
Runs .tftest.hcl files that plan or apply a module with chosen variables and check assert conditions.

review.q: Write the for_each line that gives one Spot group per size except wide.
review.a: for_each = { for k, v in var.sizes : k => v if k != "wide" }

review.q: Name two kinds of module change that are safe for existing callers, and two that are not.
review.a: Safe: adding an optional variable (with a default), adding a new resource or output. Not safe: renaming or removing a variable or output, renaming a for_each key or a resource label without a moved block.

review.q: What does a tofu test run with expect_failures = [var.warm_pool_size] prove?
review.a: That the module's validation on warm_pool_size really rejects the bad value given in that run; the run passes only if the validation fails.

remember: Read a module from its contract, treat every for_each key as an identity, and prove a change with tofu test before the plan reaches a reviewer.
